title: If a sealed interface has a `non-sealed` implementor, can an unlisted class extend it?
shortTitle: If a sealed interface has a `non-sealed` implementor, can an unlisted class extend it?
keyPoints: A `non-sealed` subtype reopens its branch, so any unlisted class may extend it freely.
The unlisted class becomes an indirect subtype of the sealed interface through the `non-sealed` type.
Sealing is enforced only at the first level: who may directly implement the sealed interface.
The compiler can no longer treat the full hierarchy as closed below a `non-sealed` branch.
In an exhaustive switch, matching the `non-sealed` base as one case covers it and all its unknown subtypes.
Use `non-sealed` deliberately for plugin architectures: a closed core with one open extension point.

s1_definition.oneliner: A `non-sealed` subtype reopens its branch, so any unlisted class may extend it and thereby become an indirect subtype of the sealed interface.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`non-sealed` reopens** – the hierarchy at that point returns to normal unrestricted extension rules.
- **Unlisted classes** – any class may extend the `non-sealed` type without appearing in any `permits` clause.
- **Transitive subtype** – the unlisted class is a subtype of the sealed interface through the `non-sealed` branch.
- **First-level enforcement** – sealing only restricts who may directly implement the sealed interface; below a `non-sealed` branch, extension is free.
- **Exhaustiveness impact** – the compiler cannot enumerate unknown subtypes of a `non-sealed` branch, but matching the `non-sealed` base in a switch covers them all.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India seals the list of who may directly be an Account: only Savings, Current, and a special Partner product. For Partner, head office stamps "open policy" (non-sealed), meaning any third-party fintech partner may build their own product on top of Partner without head office approving each one. So while nobody new can be a direct Account, anyone can build under the open Partner branch, and those partner-built products are still Accounts through Partner.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  non-sealed Branch: Open Extension Point    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│  sealed interface Account                   │
│      permits Savings, Current, Partner      │
│         │                                   │
│         ├── final Savings  (closed leaf)    │
│         │                                   │
│         ├── final Current  (closed leaf)    │
│         │                                   │
│         └── non-sealed Partner  (OPEN)      │
│             ├── WalletProduct   (unlisted)  │
│             ├── InsuranceProduct (unlisted)  │
│             └── ... (anyone can extend)     │
│                                             │
│  switch (account):                          │
│    case Savings  → ...                      │
│    case Current  → ...                      │
│    case Partner  → ... (covers all below)   │
│    // Exhaustive at permitted level ✓       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, if a permitted subtype of a sealed interface is declared `non-sealed`, any unlisted class can extend it freely. Sealing only restricts the direct implementors through the `permits` clause. Choosing `non-sealed` is a deliberate statement that this branch is reopened, and below it the normal unrestricted extension rules apply.

The unlisted class extends the `non-sealed` type and becomes a subtype of the sealed interface transitively. The sealing guarantee still holds because the unlisted class does not directly implement the sealed interface; it goes through the permitted `non-sealed` type. In a banking project at National Bank of India, Pankaj seals `Account` so only savings, current, and partner may directly be accounts. Savings and current are final, and partner is non-sealed. A wallet product from a third-party fintech extends partner without being listed anywhere, and it is still a valid Account.

The important consequence is about exhaustiveness. Because the `non-sealed` branch is open, the compiler cannot enumerate all classes beneath it. But matching the `non-sealed` base as one case in a switch covers it and all its unknown subtypes, so the switch stays exhaustive at the permitted-type level. This trades some leaf-level exhaustiveness for extensibility, by design.

The practical rule is to use `non-sealed` sparingly and deliberately. Keep the regulated core products `final`, and open exactly one branch for third-party extensions. This isolates the open point and makes it auditable rather than leaving a hole in the whole model.

Remember one sentence: a `non-sealed` subtype reopens its branch so unlisted classes can extend it freely, and they become indirect subtypes of the sealed interface through the open branch.
